title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: true election decree segregates singular persons
latin: Verum decretum electionis est segregativum singularium personarum, quos Deus aliis praeteritis ex speciali misericordia ad salutem obtinendam infallibiliter destinavit. Ipsum vocabulum eligendi hoc arguit, sub cujus formali significatione indicatur acceptio unius, altero rejecto. At in illo Arminianae electionis decreto, Quicunque crediderit, vitam aeternam obtinebit; Quicunque incredulus manserit, peribit, nulla est singularium personarum segregatio ab aliis, nulla aliarum praeteritio aut rejectio, cum Deus tali decreto cuilibet homini ex aequo salutem polliceatur, cuilibet ex aequo perditionem interminetur.
pass_a: The true decree of election is segregative of singular persons, whom God, others being passed by, from special mercy has infallibly destined to the obtaining of salvation. The very word of electing proves this, under whose formal signification is indicated the acceptance of one, the other being rejected. But in that decree of Arminian election, Whosoever shall have believed shall obtain eternal life; Whosoever shall have remained unbelieving shall perish, there is no segregation of singular persons from others, no passing by or rejection of others, since by such a decree God promises salvation equally to any man, and threatens perdition equally to any.
pass_b: The true election decree segregates singular persons — those God, others passed by, has from special mercy infallibly destined to obtain salvation. The very word elect proves it: under its formal sense one is accepted, the other rejected. But in that Arminian decree — Whoever believes shall obtain eternal life; whoever remains unbelieving shall perish — there is no segregation of singular persons, no passing by or rejection of others, since by it God promises salvation equally to anyone and threatens perdition equally to anyone.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: Hague reply — segregation of believers; Davenant restates the question
latin: Huic argumento respondent Remonstrantes in Colloquio Hagiensi, pag. 53: Segregationem credentium esse segregationem singularium personarum; agnoscunt enim credentes esse singulares personas, pag. 51. Verum si id volumus, electionem sese extendere erga personas quasdam singulares, tanquam singulares, citra ullas qualitates in ipsis consideratas, et nominatim absque consideratione fidei, tum se pernegare electionem hoc modo singulares personas respicere. Sed haec facile refelluntur. Agnoscimus credentes esse singulares personas; nam omnis actio est singularium: sed hoc decreto, Quisquis crediderit, salvus erit, segregari a Deo singulares aliquas personas ad fidem vel vitam, aliis praeteritis, id demum pernegamus.
pass_a: To this argument the Remonstrants reply in the Hague Colloquy, p. 53: that the segregation of believers is a segregation of singular persons; for they acknowledge that believers are singular persons, p. 51. But if we mean this, that election extends itself toward certain singular persons as singular, apart from any qualities considered in them, and namely without consideration of faith, then they utterly deny that election in this way regards singular persons. But these things are easily refuted. We acknowledge that believers are singular persons; for every action is of singulars: but that by this decree, Whosoever shall have believed shall be saved, some singular persons are segregated by God unto faith or life, others being passed by — that at last we deny.
pass_b: The Remonstrants answer at the Hague Colloquy (p. 53): segregation of believers is segregation of singular persons — for believers are singular persons (p. 51). If we mean election reaches certain singulars as singulars, apart from any qualities in them, and especially without regard to faith, they flatly deny election regards singulars that way. Easily answered. We grant believers are singular persons — every act is of singulars. What we deny is that by Whoever believes shall be saved God segregates some singulars unto faith or life, others passed by.

lemmas.gloss: apart from qualities / without regard to faith

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: first — Quisquis decree stands even if none or all believe; Peter = Judas
latin: Primo, quia staret hoc decretum firmum et immobile, etiamsi nemo crederet, etiamsi omnes perirent; et e contra, etiamsi omnes crederent, et omnes servarentur. Tali ergo decreto, per modum legis aut Edicti, declaratur quibus officiis praestitis liceat cuilibet vitam aeternam adire, quibus neglectis non liceat: at interim, per modum decreti practici et segregativi, nemo segregatur aut prae aliis eligitur, nemo praeteritur aut relinquitur. Si enim Judas crediderit et perseveraverit, virtute hujus decreti servabitur: Si Petrus non crediderit et perseveraverit, virtute ejusdem damnabitur. Nihil hic decernitur Petro, quod non sub eadem conditione decernitur Judae; nihil negatur Judae, quod non sub eadem conditione negatur Petro. Pari lege et conditione, huic decreto inhaereamus, omnes destinantur ad salutem, omnes excluduntur a salute. Nulla igitur in hoc decreto singularium personarum segregatio, aut aliis praeteritis electio.
pass_a: First, because this decree would stand firm and immovable, even if no one believed, even if all perished; and on the contrary, even if all believed, and all were saved. By such a decree therefore, after the manner of a law or Edict, it is declared by what duties performed it is lawful for anyone to approach eternal life, by which neglected it is not lawful: but meantime, after the manner of a practical and segregative decree, no one is segregated or elected before others, no one is passed by or left. For if Judas shall have believed and persevered, by virtue of this decree he will be saved: If Peter shall not have believed and persevered, by virtue of the same he will be damned. Nothing is here decreed for Peter that is not under the same condition decreed for Judas; nothing is denied Judas that is not under the same condition denied Peter. By equal law and condition, if we cling to this decree, all are destined to salvation, all are excluded from salvation. There is therefore in this decree no segregation of singular persons, or election with others passed by.
pass_b: First: that decree would stand firm even if no one believed and all perished — or if all believed and all were saved. As law or edict it declares by what duties done anyone may come to eternal life, and by what neglected may not. But as a practical segregating decree, no one is set apart or chosen before others, no one passed by. If Judas believes and perseveres, by it he is saved; if Peter does not, by the same he is damned. Nothing is decreed for Peter not under the same condition for Judas; nothing denied Judas not under the same for Peter. Cling to that decree on equal law, and all are destined to salvation and all excluded from it. So there is no segregation of singulars, no election with others passed by.

lemmas.gloss: as law/edict, not practical segregating decree
same condition for Peter and Judas

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: second — separation follows Peter's act, not God's segregating decree
latin: Secundo, agnoscimus juxta tenorem praedicti decreti Petrum ad vitam aeternam separandum, postquam in fide perseveraverit: sed haec separatio consequitur ex consequente et contingente actu ipsius Petri, non oritur ex segregativo decreto ipsius Dei. Suo enim actu fuit segregatus ad salutem postquam praevisus est credidisse et perseverasse, sed praedicto decreto non fuit singulariter segregatus, sive ad fidem sive ad salutem. Simili hoc illustretur. Si Rex tale decretum sanciat, Quisquis muros oppugnatae urbis ascenderit, eques fiet; quisquis terga verterit, capite plectetur, singulares personae sunt qui muros scandunt, singulares personae qui fugiunt: neque tamen tali decreto dicitur Rex elegisse singulares quasdam personas ad equestrem dignitatem, alias autem praeteriisse; sed contulisse in singulares personas; destinasse autem illam dignitatem ex aequo omnibus, sive obtinendam, si bene se gesserint, sive amittendam, si secus. Talis per omnia est illa electio Arminiana; ac proinde non habet inclusam veram et realem separationem singularium personarum.
pass_a: Secondly, we acknowledge according to the tenor of the aforesaid decree that Peter is to be separated unto eternal life after he shall have persevered in faith: but this separation follows from the consequent and contingent act of Peter himself, it does not arise from a segregative decree of God himself. For by his own act he was segregated unto salvation after he was foreseen to have believed and persevered, but by the aforesaid decree he was not singularly segregated, whether unto faith or unto salvation. Let this be illustrated by a like case. If a King should enact such a decree, Whosoever shall have climbed the walls of the besieged city shall become a knight; whosoever shall have turned his back shall be punished with death, they are singular persons who scale the walls, singular persons who flee: and yet by such a decree the King is not said to have elected certain singular persons unto knightly dignity, and to have passed by others; but to have conferred it upon singular persons; and to have destined that dignity equally to all, either to be obtained if they behave well, or to be lost if otherwise. Such in all points is that Arminian election; and therefore it does not have included a true and real separation of singular persons.
pass_b: Second: we grant that by that decree's tenor Peter is to be set apart to eternal life once he has persevered in faith — but that separation follows from Peter's own consequent contingent act, not from a segregating decree of God. By his act he was set apart to salvation after he was foreseen to have believed and persevered; by the decree itself he was not singularly segregated unto faith or salvation. Like case: if a king enacts Whoever scales the besieged city's walls shall be knighted; whoever turns his back shall die — those who climb and those who flee are singular persons; yet the king is not said to have elected certain singulars to knighthood and passed others by, but to have conferred it on singulars and destined that dignity equally to all — to be won if they behave well, lost if not. Arminian election is of that kind throughout, and so includes no true real separation of singular persons.

lemmas.gloss: king/walls analogy — equal destiny, not segregation

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: third — singulars as singularly loved; Aquinas on election and dilection
latin: Tertio, ad id quod responsum est negando, electionem sese extendere ad singulares personas qua singulares, regerimus, Nos haud affirmare hoc decretum respicere singulares qua singulares, sed qua singulariter Deo ex mera gratuita benevolentia dilectos. Vide Thomas, part. 1. qu. 23. art. 4: Praedestinatio aliquorum in salutem aeternam praesupponit, quod Deus illorum velit salutem. Ad quod pertinet electio et dilectio: Dilectio, in quantum vult iis hoc bonum salutis aeternae; Electio, in quantum hoc bonum aliquibus prae aliis vult. Et haec dilectio praesupponitur electioni.
pass_a: Thirdly, to that which was answered by denying that election extends itself to singular persons as singular, we rejoin that we by no means affirm that this decree regards singulars as singulars, but as singularly loved by God from mere gratuitous benevolence. See Thomas, Part 1, q. 23, art. 4: The predestination of some unto eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. To which pertain election and dilection: Dilection, inasmuch as he wills to them this good of eternal salvation; Election, inasmuch as he wills this good to some before others. And this dilection is presupposed to election.
pass_b: Third: to their denial that election reaches singulars as singulars, we reply we do not claim the decree regards singulars merely as singulars, but as singularly loved by God from mere gratuitous goodwill. So Aquinas (ST 1.23.4): predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. That involves dilection and election — dilection insofar as he wills them the good of eternal salvation; election insofar as he wills that good to some before others. And dilection is presupposed to election.

title: Cap. VI Arg. 12 close: faith in election as effect prepared, not presupposed cause
latin: Denique, quod dicunt electionem non tendere in singulares personas citra considerationem fidei in illis praevisae, fatemur electionem nunquam fieri absque omni consideratione bonarum qualitatum, fidei scilicet et sanctitatis: considerantur enim tanquam virtute electionis omnibus electis praeparatae et donandae. Sed non considerantur ut praesuppositae electionis decreto, tanquam causae, conditiones, aut occasiones ipsius electionis, sicut ostendunt Arminiani. Nam praedestinatio sive electio respicit quidem id quod est ex parte nostra, hoc est, fidem et obedientiam nostram, non sicut id quod inclinat voluntatem Dei ad volendum, sed sicut id ad cujus productionem Divina voluntas gratiam ordinavit. Bona enim qualitas aut operatio quaecunque in hominibus considerata non est ratio praedestinationis sed Terminus, ut bene Thomas, Comment. in Rom. 8. Consideretur ergo fides in electione, sed ut effectus, non ut ratio vel conditio electionis.
pass_a: Finally, as to what they say, that election does not tend unto singular persons apart from consideration of faith foresighted in them, we confess that election is never made without every consideration of good qualities, namely of faith and holiness: for they are considered as by virtue of election prepared and to be given to all the elect. But they are not considered as presupposed to the decree of election, as causes, conditions, or occasions of election itself, as the Arminians pretend. For predestination or election does indeed regard that which is on our part, that is, our faith and obedience, not as that which inclines the will of God to willing, but as that to whose production the Divine will has ordained grace. For any good quality or operation considered in men is not the reason of predestination but the Terminus, as Thomas well, Commentary on Romans 8. Let faith therefore be considered in election, but as effect, not as reason or condition of election.
pass_b: Finally, they say election does not reach singulars apart from foresighted faith in them. We grant election never happens without regard to good qualities — faith and holiness — but as prepared and to be given to all the elect by virtue of election. They are not presupposed to the election decree as causes, conditions, or occasions of election itself, as Arminians claim. Predestination does regard what is on our side — our faith and obedience — not as what bends God's will to will, but as that for whose production the divine will ordained grace. Any good quality or work considered in men is not the reason of predestination but its Terminus (so Aquinas on Rom. 8). Let faith be considered in election, then — as effect, not as reason or condition of election.

lemmas.gloss: qualities prepared by election, not presupposed to it
faith as effect, not reason/condition of election
